topComments.author: bratao
topComments.text: This is pretty bittersweet to see. Python is my favorite language, but I'm honestly tired of having to rewrite performance bottlenecks in Cython or Rust all the time. When the Faster CPython project started with Microsoft's backing, I was really excited. Mark Shannon had that plan promising huge speedups across a few cycles, and while that clearly turned out to be much harder than anticipated, the team still kept pushing forward to deliver a real JIT. Seeing all of that get bogged down in committee bureaucracy now is just frustrating. I have a lot of respect for the core devs and I know maintaining CPython, and it is a time donation job. It isn't easy. But I feel that over-caution and red tape ends up discouraging serious contributions. They are setting an unreasonably high bar for something that would obviously help the entire ecosystem. Just think about the sheer amount of electricity and compute power being wasted every single day running inefficient Python across millions of machines worldwide. Python really deserves a proper JIT. I genuinely hope they reconsider this.

On the other hand, it's pretty safe to say that the strict adherence to the PEP policy and all of the bureaucracy that comes with it is what makes Python a great language, for better or worse. Not to say that the technical objections were without merit, they likely very much weren't, and the debugger and instrumentation support and maintenance work sounds fairly painful on its own.

topComments.author: kannanvijayan
topComments.text: Gonna dump a technical hot take here. Python is a mature production language with a lot of users. Even before it was huge - like 20 years ago when I was in college - getting a small backwards compatible API change into a python extension module (gnu readline in my case) required convincing GvR personally that the API change was necessary. Every JIT attempt I've seen for python just tries to cut too deep in the first pass, and scope themselves too large. I believe any successful attempt at optimizing python performance from JIT will FIRST start with a 100% semantically compatible hidden type model for optimizing object property access and method dispatch. The single biggest performance delta in most dynamic language jits come from that, not from optimizing guards off of bytecode operations or from compiling to machine code. It's from converting hashtable lookups into constant-time guard + offset lookups. The hidden type model is also a hard nut to crack. It needs to perserve dict semantics which have very dynamic behaviour via the various `__*__` methods, and handle exotics scope objects since scoped name lookups are the most common ones which have their own exotic behaviours (I remember python providing some ability for callee frames to inspect caller scopes in some limited ways).

topComments.text: I like the analogy. It feels right. But I don't think it actually is, because it leans hard on the _feeling_ of failure, vs. the actual failure. The failure that actually matters here is product failure. Angry users. Security incidents. Downtime. Broken workflows. Stressed and uncomfortable developers have, historically, been a leading indicator of product failure. Software is complex and when devs can't handle the breadth of ownership + the depth of expertise at the same time, it means bad work that leads to product failure. It's not clear that agents fail in the same way, or that our collective intuition about how and when to trust agents is sufficiently developed to predict product failure in the same way. As anecdata: I know a bunch of growth-SaaS/last-batch-of-IPO companies where the devs are all stressed, the feature ship rate is up, and incidents are down. All at the same time. So yes, quick learners and just-in-time depth is important, but so is intuition about where discomfort is going to produce true failure. The discomfort isn't a feeling to throw away, simply trusting that you'll learn everything in time. Ownership requires holding a model of the system in your head and proactively steering where you dive.

jobs.title: Fazeshift | Senior Software Engineer | San Francisco, CA | ONSITE (5 days/week) | Full-time | $200k–$235k + equity
jobs.text: I’m Chris, VP Engineering at Fazeshift. We’re nine engineers plus our Founder/CTO and me, and I’m hiring someone who can help us do more, better: increase both what we can build and the quality and sophistication of the software we build. Accounts receivable sounds boring until you look under the hood. It sits at the intersection of money, business relationships, software systems of various vintages, and a huge amount of repetitive human work. Instead of giving finance teams another dashboard to stare at, we’re building AI agents that actually do the work across billing, collections, payments, cash application, and the systems connecting them. We’ve grown revenue 12x since 2024, and eight unicorns now run AR on Fazeshift. A big part of what makes the engineering interesting is that we’re intentionally not the system of record. Our customers already run on ERPs, CRMs, banks, billing systems, payment processors, spreadsheets, and internal software, so we have to understand state across systems we don’t control, act safely in them, and recover when reality disagrees with what an API says should have happened. A timeout doesn’t necessarily mean a write failed. Webhooks can arrive late or twice. A payment may not contain enough information to identify an invoice. In those cases, blindly retrying can be exactly the wrong thing to do. We use coding agents heavily ourselves. Engineers use Conductor, stacked PRs, Linear, and multiple frontier models every day, with internal skills and tooling that let agents drive and validate our local development environment. We’re especially interested in engineers whose development workflow has already materially changed because of coding agents: people who are comfortable delegating meaningful work, keeping independent threads moving in parallel, debugging where agents get stuck, and improving the surrounding system when the workflow breaks down. But generated code is still your code . Judgment, debugging, systems thinking, taste, and understanding what actually shipped matter more here, not less. Our development style is roughly: design enough to find the shape of the problem, then build to learn. There’s a short distance here between noticing a problem, deciding what should happen, building it, and seeing the result in production with our customers. You’ll own meaningful problems from ambiguity through design, implementation, rollout, and production, and you’ll work directly with the people affected by what you build. We’re looking for 5+ years of professional experience, strong TypeScript/full-stack skills, solid systems judgment, and real production ownership. No fintech background needed. Stack: TypeScript/Next.js, tRPC, Prisma/MySQL/PlanetScale, Inngest, AWS. I read every HN application myself. Email chris.zehner@fazeshift.com with HN in the subject, your LinkedIn/GitHub/résumé, and a few sentences about something interesting you’ve built or improved recently.

infoqArticles.description: Anthropic recently detailed how it migrated its monorepo from Git to Scion. Scion is a source control system that moves repository operations to the server side and uses content-addressed storage and tiered caches for agent and CI workloads. The design sacrifices offline independence for less local data and shared infrastructure. By Eran Stiller
infoqArticles.author: Eran Stiller

infoqArticles.title: Presentation: Serving LLMs at Scale: The Hidden KV Cache Advantage
infoqArticles.description: Khawaja Shams shares a distributed systems perspective on scaling LLM inference stacks efficiently. He discusses practical strategies for optimizing GPU utilization, managing KV cache memory cliffs, leveraging tiered storage, reducing tail latency, and implementing disaggregated prefill and decode architectures to improve overall fleet performance, cost economics, and availability. By Khawaja Sham
infoqArticles.author: Khawaja Shams

infoqArticles.title: AWS Shows Use of AI Agents to Triage Linux Kernel CVEs
infoqArticles.description: Engineers from Amazon Web Services (AWS) have described how the team that maintains the Linux kernel for EC2 infrastructure handles kernel CVEs. The process combines an automated filter, an AI agent and human review. The team also argues that it needs to move to newer long-term-support (LTS) kernels, as older branches collect fixes that are never backported. By Matt Saunders
infoqArticles.author: Matt Saunders

infoqArticles.title: Cloudflare and VoidZero Introduce tsrs: An AI-Generated Rust Port of TypeScript
infoqArticles.description: Cloudflare, VoidZero and Max Schwenk announced tsrs, an experimental Rust port of the TypeScript compiler, built with the TypeScript team's involvement. Cloudflare claims up to 8x faster checking and 70% less memory than TypeScript 7.0, though one test against 7.1 beta showed 2.7x. It lacks watch mode and a language server, and exits with code 2 on type errors. By Daniel Curtis
infoqArticles.author: Daniel Curtis

infoqArticles.title: Developers Reporting Double-Digit Weekly Time Savings From AI Fell From 68% to 26%
infoqArticles.description: Atlassian’s State of Developer Experience 2026 finds the share of developers saving ten or more hours a week with AI dropped from 68% to 26% year over year, while only 28% report noticeably less friction than before AI. Engineering leaders report spending more time managing and correcting AI output than developers do. By Steef-Jan Wiggers
infoqArticles.author: Steef-Jan Wiggers

infoqArticles.title: AGNTCon + MCPCon 2026: Agentic AI Foundation Adds Four Projects as MCP Turns to Security
infoqArticles.description: At AGNTCon + MCPCon North America 2026, the Agentic AI Foundation added OpenSandbox, Open Responses, Agent Skills, and OpenEnv, reaching ten projects in its first year. Keynotes from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and UC Berkeley focused on MCP in production, security, and agents with their own identities. By Andrew Hoblitzell
infoqArticles.author: Andrew Hoblitzell

infoqArticles.title: OpenTofu 1.13 Lets Module Authors Reduce Unknown Values at Plan Time
infoqArticles.description: OpenTofu 1.13 adds convert and assume... functions that let module authors give the planner type and value hints for unknown values, so more expressions resolve during tofu plan. If a value unknown during planning later violates a guarantee, OpenTofu reports an error during apply. By Mark Silvester
infoqArticles.author: Mark Silvester

infoqArticles.title: DigitalOcean Launches Learning and Data Services to Enable Self-Improving AI Agents
infoqArticles.description: DigitalOcean has announced the public preview of Learning Services and Agent Data Services, enabling developers to build, evaluate, and continuously improve AI agents within a unified, AI-native, cloud platform. By Sergio De Simone
infoqArticles.author: Sergio De Simone

infoqArticles.title: Production AI and Engineering Team Design: InfoQ’s November Certification Cohorts
infoqArticles.description: A preview of three November InfoQ online certification cohorts covering production AI systems, retrieval and agent design, engineering team flow, AI roles, and measurement, facilitated by Adi Polak, Lan Chu, and Olimpiu Pop. By Artenisa Chatziou
infoqArticles.author: Artenisa Chatziou

infoqArticles.title: Java News Roundup: JDK 28 Schedule, Oracle CPUs, eMudhra Certs, Apache POI, WildFly, Azul, BellSoft
infoqArticles.description: This week's Java roundup for October 19th, 2026, features news highlighting: the proposed release schedule for JDK 28; the eMudhra Intermediate CA certificates breach; the October 2026 Critical Patch Update; Azul and BellSoft CPUs; GA releases of WildFly 42 and Apache POI 6.0; the beta release of Open Liberty 26.0.0.11; and maintenance releases of Micronaut and JobRunr. By Michael Redlich
infoqArticles.author: Michael Redlich

infoqArticles.title: Readyon Builds Four Layer Tenant Isolation for Multi Tenant Amazon EKS
infoqArticles.description: ReadyOn has detailed a four-layer tenant isolation architecture for its Harmony platform on Amazon EKS. The design combines Kubernetes namespaces, dedicated Karpenter node pools, VPC security groups, and per-tenant Aurora databases, with controls evaluated against a 10-stage multi-tenant threat model focused on cross-tenant access and lateral movement. By Leela Kumili
infoqArticles.author: Leela Kumili

infoqArticles.title: Article: The Evolution of Agentic Harnesses: From Chains to Graph to Code
infoqArticles.description: Agentic LLM systems have moved from linear prompt chains to graph-based workflows and, more recently, code-executing harnesses. Chains are simple but fragile, graphs add branching, retries, and validation, and code harnesses verify outputs through execution. The article advises validating model outputs and choosing the least complex design that meets reliability, speed, and cost needs. By Karthik
infoqArticles.author: Karthik Ramgopal

infoqArticles.title: Cloudflare’s Auto Router Rates Each Request for Stakes, from the Most Recent Turns
infoqArticles.description: Cloudflare has released Auto Router in public beta through AI Gateway, picking a model per request from a classifier that scores complexity, ambiguity, stakes and context dependence. Cloudflare’s own benchmark puts it ten points below Claude Opus 5.5 on success rate at a third of the cost, and practitioners have questioned how stakes survive a long agent session. By Steef-Jan Wiggers
infoqArticles.author: Steef-Jan Wiggers

infoqArticles.title: MCP C# SDK 2.0 Makes HTTP Stateless by Default and Adds Multi Round-Trip Requests
infoqArticles.description: Microsoft announced version 2.0 of the official MCP C# SDK, which implements the 2026-07-28 revision of the Model Context Protocol with stateless HTTP servers by default, standardised routing headers and Multi Round-Trip Requests. Releases 2.1 to 2.3 have since added hybrid session serving, a subscriptions/listen handler and a series of discovery, OAuth and shutdown fixes. By Edin Kapić
infoqArticles.author: Edin Kapić
